nameStory: This dodder gets its species name 'saururi' from its preferred host plant, lizard's tail (Saururus cernuus), where 'saurus' means lizard in Greek. Like other dodders, it's sometimes called devil's hair or witch's hair because of its tangled, thread-like appearance that seems to magically strangle other plants. The common name 'dodder' comes from an old word meaning 'to shake or tremble,' referring to how these parasitic vines quiver in the breeze.
description: Lizard's tail dodder is a parasitic vine that looks like bright orange or yellow spaghetti draped over wetland plants. This leafless plant produces thin, thread-like stems that twist and coil around host plants, forming dense tangles that can cover entire patches of vegetation. The stems are typically 1-2mm thick and can spread several feet across suitable habitat. Like all dodders, it has no roots once mature and survives entirely by stealing nutrients from its host plants through specialized suckers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Parasitic vine with bright orange to yellow thread-like stems that form tangled masses over host plants, with no leaves or functional roots

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or cream-colored bell-shaped flowers clustered in small groups along the stems, each flower only 2-3mm wide with 5 petals

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, fleshy stems about 1-2mm thick that feel slightly sticky when fresh and coil tightly around host plants in a clockwise direction

idTips.label: Host Preference
idTips.description: Specifically targets lizard's tail plants in wetland areas, though may occasionally parasitize other nearby wetland species

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules that split open to release 2-4 tiny brown seeds with a rough, sandpaper-like texture

habitat: Found exclusively in wetland areas where its preferred host, lizard's tail, grows naturally. Look for it in shallow marshes, swamp edges, stream banks, and other permanently moist areas with rich, organic soils. In New England, this is an extremely rare plant with only a few documented locations, typically in southern areas with the right wetland conditions.

seasonality.spring: Young seedlings briefly emerge from soil before finding and attaching to host plants. Orange thread-like stems become visible as they begin climbing host vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak visibility period when bright orange tangles are most obvious against green host plants. Tiny white flowers appear in mid to late summer in dense clusters.
seasonality.fall: Stems may turn more yellow or brown as they mature. Small capsule fruits develop and split open to release seeds before first frost.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist as brown, brittle tangles on dead host plants, but living plant material dies back completely with cold weather.

funFact: This dodder is so specialized that it can actually 'smell' its preferred host plant from a distance - seedlings will grow toward the scent of lizard's tail even before making physical contact, like a plant bloodhound tracking its prey!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the more common scaldweed dodder, but lizard's tail dodder is found specifically on lizard's tail plants in wetlands, while scaldweed attacks a much wider variety of hosts in drier areas. The wetland habitat and specific host plant are your best clues - if it's not growing on lizard's tail in a marsh, it's probably a different dodder species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native plants, dodders are often mistaken for invasive species because of their parasitic nature and the way they can completely smother their hosts. However, they're actually important parts of natural ecosystems and have co-evolved with their host plants over thousands of years.
compareHints: Lizard's tail dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and highly specific host preference for lizard's tail plants. Most other dodders in our region, like scaldweed or field dodder, parasitize multiple host species and grow in drier upland areas. The wetland location and orange stems on lizard's tail plants make identification relatively straightforward when you find it.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scaldweed differs from its dodder relatives primarily in where it grows - it prefers wetter habitats than Field Dodder, and its stems tend to be slightly thicker than Five Angled Dodder.
Compared to other dodders in New England, field dodder produces the largest seeds and tends to form denser, more tangled masses.

Buttonbush Dodder differs from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and host preferences - while Field Dodder attacks crops and Scaldweed Dodder prefers woodland edges, Buttonbush Dodder is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Sessile Dodder is unique among New England dodders for specializing on woody hosts rather than soft-stemmed plants.
Smartweed Dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its habitat and host preferences - it's the wetland specialist of the dodder family.
Among New England's dodder species, hazel dodder is distinguished by its preference for woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants.
Five Angled Dodder is much rarer in New England than the common Scaldweed dodder, and prefers wetter habitats compared to Field Dodder's preference for dry agricultural areas.
